<reason>Both sides were strong. CON (A) had the sharper reframe — the motion says "courts," and it pressed hard on the wrong-organ problem, the allocation/queue problem drawn from the terrorism-exception analogy, the countermeasures/permanence contradiction, and the best single turn of the debate: recasting PRO's "manifest aggression corroborated by overwhelming collective judgment" as a headcount that means great powers are never manifest aggressors, so the power "runs downhill." PRO (B), however, held the decisive comparative frame throughout — aggressor pays versus victims and third-party taxpayers pay — and answered the two most important pressures adequately (statute defines the standard while the court makes findings on aggression, asset character, causation and proportionality; the same "who decides" problem afflicts CON's claims commission, which also needs a finding of aggression). PRO's closing crystallization landed the most damaging blow: CON's own counterplan immobilizes the corpus, pools its income and borrows against the principal, i.e. it uses the aggressor's money for reconstruction on pure say-so with no threshold, no reasons and no appeal, leaving title in Moscow and Ukraine rebuilding on credit. That converts CON's alternative from a clean rule-of-law high ground into a mechanism with the same asymmetry and less process, blunting both the legitimacy and the downhill-precedent turns. CON's reply (holding is reversible, transfer is not; holders accept political responsibility) is coherent but only partially restores the gap. CON also incurred a real execution cost: two turns, including the opening and second rebuttal, were clipped so their concluding weighing was lost, while PRO delivered complete speeches inside the caps. CON keeps a genuinely live edge on the queue/rival-creditor point, which PRO never fully solved, but PRO offered the cleaner, easier-to-decide path.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing parity turn: showing that CON's own remedy immobilizes, monetizes and borrows against Russian reserves with no judicial finding at all, so the debate was never courts versus restraint but two ways of using the same money — one with proof of aggression and appeal, one without. That materially undercut CON's legitimacy and irreversibility framing, which CON could only partly repair with the holding-versus-extinguishing-title distinction.</best_rebuttal>
